methodological_rigor.justification: This is a large retrospective cohort across an entire state oncology network using deterministic linkage between the Hospital Cancer Registry and the Mortality Information System, with follow-up through December 31, 2021 and a clearly defined breast cancer-specific mortality endpoint (ICD-10 C50.x). Eligibility criteria, cohort size (12,096 for descriptive/survival analyses), and censoring rules (other-cause deaths censored in cause-specific models) are specified, supporting an appropriate design for prognostic/disparity questions. The statistical approach is generally strong: Kaplan-Meier estimation with log-rank testing, proportional hazards checking (with exclusion of variables that violated assumptions), and multivariable cause-specific Cox models reporting HRs with 95% CIs. Key limitations are acknowledged in the methods/results, including substantial missingness in several registry variables and reliance on complete-case multivariable analysis (7,191/12,096), which may introduce selection bias and residual confounding in comparisons such as public vs private referral source.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The study is an individual observational cohort (registry-linked retrospective cohort), which corresponds to Oxford LoE 2b. Its endpoints are directly patient-relevant (breast cancer-specific mortality and 5-year survival by stage) and the findings have clear health-system implications, quantifying large survival gradients by stage (e.g., 5-year survival near 97% in stage I vs ~32% in stage IV) and by referral pathway (private vs public system HR 0.83). Although not an interventional study, the results are clinically and policy relevant for prioritizing early diagnosis and addressing access inequities within an oncology care network. Generalizability is still constrained by reliance on a hospital registry population and incomplete covariate capture typical of secondary data.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is appropriate for this cohort study, and the manuscript explicitly states it was reported following STROBE recommendations. Reporting is relatively thorough for registry-linked observational work, including setting description (CACON/UNACON network), explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, linkage procedures (identifiers used and manual review), outcome definition using SIM underlying cause of death, and key analytic choices (cause-specific Cox, proportional hazards assessment, and rationale for not using multiple imputation). Some reporting gaps remain, including potential selection effects from complete-case analysis and limited detail on timing of treatments (noted as a source of immortal time bias in the discussion). Data and code availability are not described in the blinded text; the data originate from restricted administrative registries and analyses were performed in R/RStudio without shared code or datasets, suggesting limited reproducibility access.

novelty_literature.justification: The work is a meaningful empirical extension by linking statewide hospital cancer registry records to a mortality system to estimate breast cancer-specific survival and evaluate prognostic factors across an entire oncology care network. The conceptual framing (stage-driven survival disparities and public-private access gradients) is well established, but the scale (statewide network) and linkage-based mortality ascertainment provide added value beyond single-center cohorts. The analysis also uses referral source as an access-pathway proxy and documents substantial incompleteness patterns in registry variables, which strengthens its positioning for surveillance and quality improvement. Overall, it is more than a minor replication but remains within established observational epidemiology rather than introducing a new method or mechanism.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly structured, with an abstract that provides the cohort definition, follow-up window, main methods (Kaplan-Meier and cause-specific Cox), and key quantitative results including HRs with confidence intervals. Methods are generally transparent, including linkage procedures, variable definitions, and justification for key analytic decisions (e.g., excluding variables that violated proportional hazards and not applying multiple imputation). Results are readable and interpretability is supported by explicit reporting of survival estimates by stage and referral source, with figures/tables appropriately captioned for what is available in this normalized format. Some sections are dense and occasionally repetitive (e.g., duplicated inclusion/exclusion bullets), but overall presentation supports evaluation.

key_strengths: Large statewide cohort (12,096 women) spanning all hospitals in a defined oncology network with long administrative follow-up through December 31, 2021.
Registry-to-mortality deterministic linkage is described in detail and enables breast cancer-specific mortality estimation beyond single-institution ascertainment.

Appropriate survival methods for the question: Kaplan-Meier estimates with log-rank testing and multivariable cause-specific Cox modeling with proportional hazards assessment and reporting of HRs with 95% CIs.
Findings have clear clinical/policy relevance, quantifying strong stage-at-diagnosis gradients and referral pathway (public vs private) disparities.
key_concerns: Heavy missingness in several registry variables and reliance on complete-case multivariable analysis (7,191/12,096) could bias effect estimates and limits interpretability for access-pathway comparisons.
Residual confounding is likely for public-private comparisons because socioeconomic and diagnostic/treatment-timing variables are incompletely captured in secondary registries.
Treatment variables are difficult to interpret causally without treatment timing; the manuscript notes potential immortal time bias but does not model time-dependent treatment receipt.
chief_reviewer.rationale: Given the large linked cohort, clear clinical relevance, and generally appropriate survival modeling, this is plausibly acceptable at a tier-2 oncology journal with minor revisions focused on clarifying missing-data impacts and strengthening causal-interpretation cautions for treatment and referral pathway effects.
